questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an assumption made in analysing the motion of projectiles?
questions.answer: The horizontal and vertical components are treated as independent.
options: Horizontal and vertical components are dependent on each other
A constant acceleration due to gravity

questions.question: Planet Falcon is 12 times more massive than Planet Unicorn and has a radius 4 times that of Unicorn. What is the ratio of the gravitational acceleration at the surface of Falcon to that of Unicorn?
questions.answer: $g\propto\dfrac{M}{r^2}=\dfrac{12}{16}=\dfrac34$.

questions.question: A long straight current-carrying wire is shown. What is the direction of the magnetic field at point P?
questions.answer: By the right-hand grip rule, below a current flowing to the right the field is into the page.

questions.question: A bar magnet is moved into a conducting wire ring as shown. Which of the following would increase the induced current in the ring?
questions.answer: A faster magnet changes the flux more rapidly, giving a larger emf and current.
options: Increasing the speed of the magnet
Reversing the polarity of the bar magnet
Moving the magnet away from the ring

questions.question: Which of the following would increase the torque on the coil in a simple DC motor?
questions.answer: $\tau=nIAB\sin\theta$. For a given supply voltage, less resistance means more current.
options: Reversing the direction of the current
Decreasing the area of the coil
Decreasing the resistance of the coil
Decreasing the strength of the magnetic field

questions.question: When a current flows through the coil shown, the total flux through its interior is 80 mWb. The cross-section is 5 cm × 10 cm. What is the magnetic field strength through the interior of the coil?
When examining stellar spectra, what information does the wavelength shift in the diagram provide?
questions.answer: A shift of all the lines is a Doppler shift due to motion of the star towards or away from the observer.

questions.question: A teacher swings a bucket of water in a vertical circle above their head. Why does the bucket have to stay above a certain speed to ensure the water does not fall out?
questions.answer: At the top, if $v^2/r\ge g$ the bucket accelerates downwards at least as fast as the water would fall, so they stay together with the same acceleration.
options: To ensure there is enough lift to counteract the force of gravity
So that there is the same acceleration for the bucket and the water
To allow the water to have no weight

questions.question: A thin metal rod carries a current as shown. In which direction will the rod experience a force?
questions.answer: The current is into the page and the field is to the right (N to S), so the force is down the page.

questions.question: Two satellites of equal mass are in stable circular orbits at X and Y, as shown to scale. What is the ratio of the kinetic energy of the satellite at X to that at Y?
questions.answer: $K=\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\propto\dfrac1r$. Measured from Earth's centre, $r_Y\approx1.5\,r_X$.

questions.question: A deuterium nucleus (1 proton and 1 neutron) is placed between the charged plates shown, touching the centre of the positive plate. How much work is done by the electric field if the nucleus is allowed to move under its influence?
Which of the following phenomena could not be accounted for by Newton's model of light?
questions.answer: Interference requires wave superposition, which a particle model cannot produce.

questions.question: Ganymede, a moon of Jupiter, has mass $1.48\times10^{23}$ kg and radius 2600 km. It has an orbital speed of 10.8 km s$^{-1}$ and an orbital radius of $1.07\times10^3$ km. What is the gravitational force of Ganymede on Jupiter?
questions.answer:
$F=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}=\dfrac{1.48\times10^{23}\times(1.08\times10^4)^2}{1.07\times10^6}=1.61\times10^{25}$ N.

*Note: the orbital radius printed in the paper is a misprint (the real value is about $1.07\times10^6$ km, which would give A). The answer shown uses the printed data.*

questions.question: A mass on a banked track is in circular motion at a constant height. Which expression describes the centripetal force due to the banked track?
questions.answer: The horizontal component of the normal force points to the centre.

questions.question: The coil in the generator shown is rotated through 2 revolutions from the position shown. Which graph best represents the current through the external resistance?
questions.answer: Slip rings give a continuous alternating current: two full cycles of equal amplitude for two revolutions.

questions.question: Conducting plates swing freely between two opposite magnetic poles. Plate A has segments cut out of it. Which best describes what occurs?
questions.answer: The slots in A break up eddy current paths, so B experiences greater magnetic damping.
options: Plate A comes to rest more quickly due to the repulsive interaction between eddy currents and the external field.
Plate B oscillates more quickly due to Lenz's law.
Plate A is laminated, which restricts the size of eddy currents, causing it to slow down more quickly.
Plate B has larger eddy currents induced in it (Faraday's law) than Plate A, so it comes to rest more quickly.

questions.question: The visible emission lines of hydrogen (the Balmer series) are shown. What is the frequency of the longest wavelength light in the series?
questions.answer: $f=\dfrac{c}{\lambda}=\dfrac{3.00\times10^8}{656\times10^{-9}}=4.6\times10^{14}$ Hz.

questions.question: A simple DC motor is run as a generator by manually rotating the coil as shown. Which of the following is true?
questions.answer: The emf in the coil is alternating. The split ring only keeps the output at the brushes in one direction.
options: Current flows in the direction B to A
The commutator ensures a direct current is generated in the coil
The current constantly reverses direction in the coil as it rotates
The voltage at the brushes constantly reverses

questions.question: Light of wavelength 540 nm passes through the slits shown (slit separation 0.15 mm). The distance between the central bright band and the first bright band is 1.5 cm. What is the distance $d$ between the double slit and the screen?
questions.answer: $d=\dfrac{y\,s}{\lambda}=\dfrac{0.015\times1.5\times10^{-4}}{540\times10^{-9}}\approx4.2$ m, where $s$ is the slit separation.

questions.question: Faraday's first electric motor is shown. A solid conducting rod XY rotates continually in a clockwise direction. Which change would decrease the period of rotation of the rod?
questions.answer: AC would make the rod oscillate and reversing the magnet only reverses the direction. A shorter rod has a smaller moment of inertia about X and a shorter path for each revolution.
options: Reversing the polarity of the magnet

questions.question: A 500 g toy falcon is to be launched into space. Calculate its weight on the surface of the Earth.
questions.answer: $W=mg=0.500\times9.8=4.9$ N (towards the centre of the Earth).

questions.question: Derive the expression for escape velocity by considering gravitational potential energy. Explain the steps of your derivation.
questions.answer:
Escape velocity is the minimum launch speed for an unpowered object to reach an infinite distance, where $U=0$, arriving with zero kinetic energy.

The gravitational potential energy at distance $r$ from the centre of a planet of mass $M$ is $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$.

By conservation of mechanical energy, $K_i+U_i=K_f+U_f$:
$$\tfrac12mv^2-\frac{GMm}{r}=0+0$$
so $\tfrac12v^2=\dfrac{GM}{r}$ and
$$v_{esc}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}}$$
It is independent of the mass of the projectile.

questions.question: Does a 500 g toy falcon need to reach the escape velocity of the Earth to be launched into space? Justify your answer.
questions.answer: No. Escape velocity applies to an unpowered object that must get infinitely far away. A rocket with continuing thrust can carry the falcon into space at any speed, and an object in orbit is in space while still gravitationally bound to Earth, at less than escape speed.

questions.question: Fireworks are launched from a tower at 50 m s$^{-1}$, $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. The launch point is 305 m above the ground and the fireworks explode 280 m above the ground. Calculate the horizontal distance from the tower at which they explode.
questions.answer:
$u_y=50\sin30^\circ=25$ m s$^{-1}$ and $s_y=-25$ m:
$$-25=25t-4.9t^2\Rightarrow t=5.96\text{ s}$$
$s_x=50\cos30^\circ\times5.96\approx258$ m.

questions.question: Fireworks are launched from a tower at 50 m s$^{-1}$, $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. The launch point is 305 m above the ground and the fireworks explode 280 m above the ground. Describe quantitatively how increasing the launch angle to $45^\circ$ would change the situation.
questions.answer:
Assume they still explode 280 m above the ground. At $45^\circ$, $u_x=u_y=35.4$ m s$^{-1}$.

- Time of flight: $-25=35.4t-4.9t^2\Rightarrow t=7.86$ s (up from 5.96 s).
- Horizontal distance: $35.4\times7.86\approx278$ m (up from 258 m).
- Maximum height above ground: $305+\dfrac{35.4^2}{19.6}\approx369$ m (up from 337 m).

(If instead a timed fuse fires after the same 5.96 s, the explosion is about 211 m away and 342 m above the ground.)

questions.question: A tungsten light bulb filament at 2800 K is approximately a black body. Using Wien's law, plot a curve representing the electromagnetic spectrum emitted by the bulb.
questions.answer:
$$\lambda_{max}=\frac{b}{T}=\frac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{2800}=1.035\times10^{-6}\text{ m}$$
The curve of intensity against wavelength rises steeply from zero, peaks at about 1035 nm (infrared) and has a long tail towards longer wavelengths.

questions.question: A proton moves horizontally at 1.5 m s$^{-1}$ through a hall containing a vertical electric field of 0.001 V m$^{-1}$ and a horizontal magnetic field of 0.02 mT perpendicular to its velocity. The two forces are in the same direction. What is the acceleration of the proton at that instant?
questions.answer:
$F=qE+qvB=1.602\times10^{-19}\left(0.001+1.5\times2\times10^{-5}\right)=1.65\times10^{-22}$ N

$a=\dfrac{F}{m}=\dfrac{1.65\times10^{-22}}{1.673\times10^{-27}}\approx9.9\times10^4$ m s$^{-2}$, in the direction of the forces. (Gravity is negligible.)

questions.question: An aluminium ring of resistance $2\ \Omega$ and diameter 15 cm rotates in a uniform magnetic field of 0.04 T, as shown, with constant angular velocity 15 rad s$^{-1}$. What maximum current flows in the ring?
questions.answer:
$\Phi=BA\cos\omega t$, so $\varepsilon=-\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}=BA\omega\sin\omega t$ and $\varepsilon_{max}=BA\omega$.

$A=\pi(0.075)^2=1.77\times10^{-2}$ m$^2$

$\varepsilon_{max}=0.04\times1.77\times10^{-2}\times15=1.06\times10^{-2}$ V

$I_{max}=\dfrac{\varepsilon_{max}}{R}=5.3\times10^{-3}$ A.

*Note: the school's answer of 3.4 mA is the average current over a quarter turn, not the maximum.*

questions.question: A transformer is labelled: Input 120 V, 60 Hz, 0.55 A; Output 12 V AC, 12 W. Explain the principle by which transformers operate, referring to the quantities on the label.
questions.answer:
- Alternating current in the primary coil produces a continually changing magnetic flux, which the iron core links to the secondary coil. By Faraday's law, $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, this induces an emf in the secondary. A steady DC would not.
- **60 Hz:** the frequency of the input. The flux, and so the output, alternates at the same 60 Hz.
- **120 V input, 12 V AC output:** a step-down transformer, with $\dfrac{N_p}{N_s}=\dfrac{V_p}{V_s}=10$.
- **12 W output:** the secondary current is $12/12=1.0$ A. An ideal transformer would draw $12/120=0.10$ A.
- **0.55 A input:** this rating (up to 66 VA) is well above 0.10 A, showing it is not ideal (or that it is a maximum rating): energy is lost to winding resistance, eddy currents, hysteresis and incomplete flux linkage.

questions.question:
In a novel, two planets orbit the star Quill, of mass $7.5\times10^4$ 'pet'. Their orbits are:

| Planet | Period ('rics') | Radius ('orts') |
|---|---|---|
| Dra | 15 | 9 |
| Groo | 20 | 12 |

Assess whether the planets orbit in accordance with Kepler's third law.
questions.answer:
Kepler's third law: for bodies orbiting the same central mass, $\dfrac{T^2}{r^3}$ is the same, whatever units are used.

- Dra: $\dfrac{15^2}{9^3}=0.31$
- Groo: $\dfrac{20^2}{12^3}=0.23$

The ratios differ significantly, so these planets do **not** obey Kepler's third law.

questions.question: Critically evaluate the role of experimental measurements, especially in how the ampere was defined and in the development of our understanding of the speed of light.
questions.answer:
**The ampere.** Until 2019 it was defined through an interaction that can be measured: the constant current in two long parallel wires 1 m apart that produces a force of $2\times10^{-7}$ N per metre, from $\dfrac{F}{l}=\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\dfrac{I_1I_2}{r}$. Current balances realised it, but only to limited precision. In May 2019 it was redefined by fixing the elementary charge, $e=1.602176634\times10^{-19}$ C, which earlier measurements had determined very precisely.

**Speed of light.**
- Galileo (lanterns): showed only that light was too fast for the method to measure.
- Rømer (1676): delays in eclipses of Io showed light has a finite speed (about $2\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$).
- Bradley (1729): stellar aberration gave about $3\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$.
- Fizeau (1849, toothed wheel) and Foucault (1862, rotating mirror): increasingly precise terrestrial values.
- Maxwell predicted $c=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}$ from electrical and magnetic measurements. Its agreement with the optical measurements was strong evidence that light is an electromagnetic wave.
- Since 1983 $c$ has been fixed at 299 792 458 m s$^{-1}$ and is used to define the metre.

**Evaluation.** Measurement was essential: it tested theory (Maxwell), overturned assumptions (that light is instantaneous) and underpins the unit system. Its value is limited by precision and by the interpretation supplied by theory; Rømer's value, for example, depended on poorly known orbital distances. As measurements became more precise than the definitions themselves, constants were fixed instead. Experiment and theory therefore develop each other.

*Note: the school's sample answer credits Galileo with a measurement of $3\times10^3$ m s$^{-1}$; he obtained no value.*

questions.question: Liz and Jack investigate the intensity of light transmitted through a polariser and analyser. Unpolarised light of intensity 650 lux is incident. Their results (relative angle: intensity) are $0^\circ$: 314; $20^\circ$: 240; $40^\circ$: 200; $60^\circ$: 105; $80^\circ$: 50; $90^\circ$: 15 lux. Compute the theoretical transmitted intensity at each angle.
questions.answer:
The polariser transmits half the unpolarised light, 325 lux. By Malus' law $I=325\cos^2\theta$:

| Angle | $0^\circ$ | $20^\circ$ | $40^\circ$ | $60^\circ$ | $80^\circ$ | $90^\circ$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Theoretical (lux) | 325 | 287 | 191 | 81 | 9.8 | 0 |

questions.question: Liz and Jack investigate the intensity of light transmitted through a polariser and analyser. Unpolarised light of intensity 650 lux is incident. Their results (relative angle: intensity) are $0^\circ$: 314; $20^\circ$: 240; $40^\circ$: 200; $60^\circ$: 105; $80^\circ$: 50; $90^\circ$: 15 lux. Graph both the experimental data and the theoretical values on the same axes.
questions.answer: Plot angle (degrees) horizontally and intensity (lux) vertically, with a title, labelled axes with units, a scale filling most of the grid, the theoretical points joined by a smooth $\cos^2$ curve and the experimental points marked distinctly (see graph).

questions.question: Liz and Jack investigate the intensity of light transmitted through a polariser and analyser. Unpolarised light of intensity 650 lux is incident. Their results (relative angle: intensity) are $0^\circ$: 314; $20^\circ$: 240; $40^\circ$: 200; $60^\circ$: 105; $80^\circ$: 50; $90^\circ$: 15 lux. Assess the accuracy of their data and suggest reasons for any difference from theory.
questions.answer: The data have limited accuracy. The general decrease agrees with Malus' law, but values differ considerably from theory: about 16% low at $20^\circ$, about 30% high at $60^\circ$ and five times too high at $80^\circ$, with 15 lux where none is expected. Likely causes are background light (a systematic offset), imperfect polarising sheets and errors in setting the angle.

questions.question: A rectangular coil is pivoted at its middle, 30 cm from each end. Side X (20 cm long) lies in a magnetic field and masses can be hung from side Y. Describe a method to investigate the effect of current on the force on side X and so validate $F_X=BIL$. Include an empty results table.
questions.answer:
**Variables:** independent: current $I$; dependent: force on X; controlled: field $B$, length $L$ in the field, position of the coil and pivot.

1. Add a variable resistor and an ammeter to the circuit. Connect the supply so that the force on X is downwards, which tends to lift Y.
2. With the switch open, balance the coil horizontally.
3. Measure $L$ and measure $B$ at side X with a magnetic field probe.
4. Hang a known small mass $m$ on Y, close the switch and adjust the current until the coil is level again. Record $I$.
5. Because the arms are equal (30 cm each), $F_X=mg$.
6. Repeat for at least five masses (for example 50, 100, 150, 200, 250 mg), three trials each, and average. Open the switch between readings to limit heating.
7. Plot $F_X$ against $I$. A straight line through the origin with gradient equal to $BL$ validates $F=BIL$.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline m\ \text{(kg)} & F=mg\ \text{(N)} & I_1\ \text{(A)} & I_2\ \text{(A)} & I_3\ \text{(A)} & I_{av}\ \text{(A)}\\ \hline & & & & & \\ \hline & & & & & \\ \hline & & & & & \\ \hline\end{array}$$

questions.question: A rectangular coil is pivoted at its middle, 30 cm from each end. Side X (20 cm long) lies in a magnetic field and masses can be hung from side Y. Explain the limitations of an investigation of $F_X=BIL$ using this equipment and set-up.
questions.answer:
- The field around X is not uniform and fringes at its edges, so the effective length in the field is uncertain.
- Force is measured indirectly by balancing small discrete masses; friction at the pivot and judging when the coil is level limit sensitivity.
- The single cell gives no fine control of current, and heating and cell run-down make the current drift.
- No means of measuring current or field is shown, so $F=BIL$ cannot be checked quantitatively without an ammeter and a field probe.
- Stray fields (including from the leads and Earth) may add small forces.

questions.question: With reference to a specific first-hand investigation from the Year 12 Physics course, describe how you would assess the reliability of your data.
questions.answer: For example, in a projectile motion investigation measuring the range of a ball launched at a fixed angle and speed: repeat the launch at least five times with identical settings and compare the ranges. The data are reliable if the repeated values are close (small spread relative to the mean). Identify any outliers, then average the consistent values to reduce random error.
